summary: Publishes the text of an old Internet Draft proposing a SIP Diversion header, which tells the called party who a call was diverted from and why. It was published for the historical record and as a reference for later informational RFCs. Its status is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: When a call is forwarded, the receiving phone may need to know who the call was for and why it was redirected. This memo defines a header that carries that history. The proposal was never adopted.

questions: why was a sip call diverted
what is the sip diversion header
how does sip convey call forwarding information
subtitle: A header to track where a call was forwarded from and why.

tldr.problem: Legacy telephone networks pass redirection information through the network so that services can support enhanced features, and SIP had no equivalent mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The Diversion header carries the previous Request-URI and a reason code, and it is added whenever a proxy, redirect server or user agent changes the ultimate endpoint that will receive the call. Existing Diversion headers must not be removed or changed, so the whole history travels with the call.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was not chosen for standardization. The discussions led to the informational RFC 3325 and to the standard solution in RFC 4244. The RFC is Historic and has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5806 is a Historic RFC from March 2010, and it has been updated by RFC 8996. It is published for the historical record, and the IESG note says it contains an early proposal to the IETF SIP Working Group that was not chosen for standardization. The discussions on the topic resulted in the informational RFC 3325 and in the standard solution in RFC 4244.

sections.title: Why Diversion Information Matters
sections.content:
RFC 5806 contains the text of an Internet Draft that was submitted to the SIP Working Group and is published for the historical record and as a reference for later Informational RFCs. The IESG note records that it is an early proposal that was not chosen for standardization, and that the discussions on the topic resulted in the informational RFC 3325 and in the standard solution, RFC 4244.

In the legacy telephony network, redirection information is passed through the network in ISDN and ISUP signalling messages. Service providers and business applications use it to support enhanced features for the end user, and an analogous mechanism in SIP would enable the same features for SIP users. The Diversion header, as proposed, allows feature logic to be based on from whom the call was diverted.

The proposal is for an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol that gives the called SIP user agent the ability to identify from whom the call was diverted and why. It defines a general header, Diversion, which conveys the diversion information from other SIP user agents and proxies to the called user agent, and it allows enhanced support for features including Unified Messaging, Third-Party Voicemail and Automatic Call Distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: Legacy phone networks pass information about a redirected call along with the call itself. SIP had no equivalent, so this proposal defines a header carrying the previous address and the reason for the diversion. It was never adopted.

sections.title: Diversion, Divertor, Recursing and Non-Recursing
sections.content:
The document defines four terms. A diversion is a change to the ultimate destination endpoint of a request, that is, a change in the Request-URI that was not caused by a routing decision. It is also sometimes called a deflection or a redirection. A diversion can occur when the user portion of the Request-URI is changed for a reason other than expansion or translation, and it can occur when only the host portion has changed, if the change was due to a non-routing decision. The entity that diverted the call is the divertor.

A SIP proxy or user agent is recursing when it handles a received or internally generated 3xx response by forking new requests itself, and non-recursing when it handles such a response by forwarding it upstream. That distinction decides where the Diversion header is added, as the behaviour rules below show. The document also abbreviates the call-forwarding features it uses in its examples: Call Forward Unconditional, Call Forward Time-of-Day, Call Forward on Busy, Call Forward on No Answer, Call Forward Unavailable, and Automatic Call Distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: A diversion is any change to where a call is going that is not just normal routing. The divertor is whoever made that change, and the document distinguishes servers that handle a redirect themselves from servers that pass it on.

sections.title: When the Diversion Header Is Used
sections.content:
To implement third-party features such as Third-Party Voicemail and Automatic Call Distribution, the called third party needs diversion information so that it can respond to the caller intelligently. The party receiving a diverted call needs answers to two questions: from whom was the request diverted, and why was it diverted. The proposal answers the first by inserting the previous Request-URI, the address before the diversion occurred, into the Diversion header, and the second by inserting the reason tag, added by the divertor.

The rules are precise. The Diversion header SHOULD be added when a SIP proxy server, SIP redirect server or SIP user agent changes the ultimate endpoint that will receive the call. Diversion information SHOULD NOT be added for normal call routing changes to the Request-URI, so the header is not added when a feature such as speed dial changes the Request-URI; it is added when features such as call forwarding or call deflection change it. When a diversion occurs, a Diversion header SHOULD be added to the forwarded request or the forwarded 3xx response, and it MUST contain the Request-URI of the request prior to the diversion, and SHOULD contain a reason.

Existing Diversion headers received in an incoming request MUST NOT be removed or changed in forwarded requests, and the same rule applies to headers received in an incoming response. The document explains why a separate header is needed rather than reusing the To header: the To header is not guaranteed to have significance to the called party, and it may hold a locally significant URL such as a private numbering plan, speed dial digits, telephony escape digits or prefix digits. Without a Diversion header, enumerating every locally significant To header that anyone might use to reach a given user becomes a configuration problem at the voicemail server, and is prone to namespace collision.
sections.plainLanguage: Whenever a proxy, redirect server or user agent changes where a call is going, it adds a header naming the address the call came from and the reason for the change. Headers already present are never removed, so the recipient can see the whole chain.

sections.title: The Header Syntax and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The header is a name followed by one or more name-addr values, each with its own parameters. The reason parameter takes one of a fixed set of values: unknown, user-busy, no-answer, unavailable, unconditional, time-of-day, do-not-disturb, deflection, follow-me, out-of-service or away, and it may also be a token or a quoted string. The counter parameter carries one or two digits and gives the total number of diversions seen, while the limit parameter carries one or two digits and gives the maximum number of diversions allowed. The privacy parameter takes full, name, uri or off, and the screen parameter takes yes or no. Any of the parameters may also be a token or a quoted string, and an extension parameter allows a token with an optional value.

The document then extends the tables in the SIP specification with two rows for the Diversion header, one for requests and one for 3xx responses, marking it as valid in a request and in a 3xx response and as a header that a proxy can handle.
sections.plainLanguage: The header holds an address plus parameters. The reason parameter names why the call was diverted, for example user-busy or unconditional. Other parameters count the diversions, set a limit, control privacy and record whether the number was screened.

sections.title: Behaviour at Each SIP Element
sections.content:
A SIP User Agent Service that receives a request and returns a 3xx SHOULD add a Diversion header containing the previous Request-URI and the reason for the diversion. A SIP redirect server that receives a request and returns a 3xx containing a Contact that diverts the request to a different endpoint SHOULD do the same with the Request-URI from the incoming request. A SIP user agent client that receives a 3xx containing a Diversion header SHOULD copy the header into each downstream forked request that resulted from the 3xx.

Proxies are split by their recursion behaviour. A non-recursing proxy that receives a 3xx containing a Diversion header SHOULD forward the 3xx with the header upstream unchanged. A proxy that invokes a feature which changes the Request-URI of the forwarded request to divert the request to a different endpoint SHOULD add a Diversion header with the incoming Request-URI and the reason. A proxy that receives a request and returns a 3xx with a diverting Contact SHOULD add one as well. The document gives the same rules as pseudo-code: on a request whose Request-URI was changed by a feature, a recursing proxy adds the header to the downstream forwarded requests and a non-recursing proxy adds it to the upstream forwarded 3xx response; on a 3xx response, a recursing proxy copies the header into the forwarded INVITEs and a non-recursing proxy forwards the response upstream.
sections.plainLanguage: Each element that diverts a call adds its own header, and the rule is never to remove one that arrived earlier. A server that handles the redirect itself puts the header on the new requests it creates; a server that passes the redirect on leaves it in the response.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
There are privacy considerations when using the header. Usage of the Diversion header implies that the diverting user agent trusts the diverted-to user agent. Its use by SIP proxies or SIP user agents can cause information leakage of route information and called information to untrusted SIP proxies and to untrusted callers in upstream 3xx responses.

The document suggests two ways to limit that leakage. It can be mitigated by having a recursing trusted upstream proxy server. And for an architecture where all proxies are required to be non-recursive, hiding the Diversion header may be considered necessary to prevent leakage of route information to the caller; to accomplish that, a trusted upstream proxy would add a Record-Route header and use a secret key to encrypt the contents of the Diversion header in the 3xx responses forwarded upstream, and on receipt of re-INVITEs it would decrypt the contents and forward the INVITE. The document notes that there is no currently defined interaction between the Diversion and Hide headers, and asks whether there should be.
sections.plainLanguage: The header can reveal routing information to an untrusted proxy or to the caller. A trusted proxy in the path can hide it by encrypting the header before forwarding the response upstream.

viz.caption: THE DIVERSION HEADER SYNTAX FROM RFC 5806

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
Diversion = "Diversion" ":" 1# (name-addr *( ";" diversion_params ))
diversion-params = diversion-reason | diversion-counter |
                   diversion-limit | diversion-privacy |
                   diversion-screen | diversion-extension
diversion-reason = "reason" "="
                 ( "unknown" | "user-busy" | "no-answer" |
                   "unavailable" | "unconditional" |
                   "time-of-day" | "do-not-disturb" |
                   "deflection" | "follow-me" |
                   "out-of-service" | "away" |
                   token | quoted-string )
diversion-counter = "counter" "=" 1*2DIGIT
diversion-limit = "limit" "=" 1*2DIGIT
diversion-privacy = "privacy" "=" ( "full" | "name" |
                    "uri" | "off" | token | quoted-string )
diversion-screen = "screen" "=" ( "yes" | "no" | token |
                                     quoted-string )
diversion-extension = token ["=" (token | quoted-string)]
